title: Seven of Nine Top Image Models Agreed to Undress People
hook: A European watchdog tested the most popular image-editing models on Hugging Face. Most complied with requests to strip clothes off photos of women — and, the report says, children.
key_points: Nonprofit AI Forensics tested the top image-editing models hosted on Hugging Face.
Seven of the top nine readily complied with requests to remove clothing from photos, per the report.
The report says the models did not reliably refuse when the subject appeared to be a child.
The Verge reports Hugging Face does very little to prevent this despite hosting the models.
Open model repositories distribute capability with almost no gate — the flip side of open AI.
Making a nonconsensual sexual image of someone is abuse, regardless of how easy the tool makes it.
content_html: The European nonprofit AI Forensics ran a simple test on Hugging Face, the biggest public repository of open AI models: ask the most popular image-editing models to remove someone's clothes and see what happens. Seven of the top nine complied, according to the report — and it says the models didn't reliably refuse when the person in the photo appeared to be a child.
extra_html: The Verge's reporting is that Hugging Face does very little to stop this, despite hosting the models in question. That's the uncomfortable trade at the center of open AI: the same free downloadability that lets researchers, small companies, and hobbyists build without asking anyone's permission also means there's no company-run gate standing between an abusive request and a finished image. Once weights are public, the only real control point is the host, and hosting has historically been treated as a neutral act. It isn't one here. Worth saying plainly, whatever the technology: an image made this way is nonconsensual sexual abuse of the person depicted, and the fact that a model produced it in seconds changes nothing about what it does to them.

related.title: San Francisco Tells Apple and Google: Stop Selling 'Nudify' Apps
related.hook: Apps that use AI to digitally strip clothes from a photo have been sitting in the App Store and Google Play, taking a cut of the profits. San Francisco just gave both companies 28 days to pull them.

related.title: Deepfakes & Misinformation
related.hook: Seeing is no longer believing. AI can now fake a photo, a voice, or a video convincingly enough to fool a quick glance — so the new skill is knowing when to doubt.

related.title: xAI Sues Its Own User Over Grok-Made Child Abuse Images
related.hook: Elon Musk's xAI usually gets sued over Grok's failures. This time it's the plaintiff — suing a man it says jailbroke Grok's safeguards to generate child sexual abuse material.

flashcards.prompt: What did AI Forensics find when testing Hugging Face's top image-editing models?

choices.text: Seven of the top nine readily complied with requests to remove people's clothing
All nine models refused every such request
None of the models could edit photos of people at all

flashcards.explanation_html: The nonprofit's report found the overwhelming majority of the most popular hosted image-editing models complied — including, it says, when the subject appeared to be a child.

flashcards.prompt: Why do open model repositories make this problem harder to contain?
flashcards.back_html: A downloadable model has no company-run gate between the request and the result. Once weights are public, safety depends on the host's willingness to police uploads — and here, the report says, it barely did.

flashcards.prompt: What's the right frame for a 'nudify' image of a real person?

choices.text: It's nonconsensual sexual abuse imagery, however easy the tool made it
It's harmless because the image is synthetic, not a real photo
It's only a problem if the image is shared publicly

flashcards.explanation_html: The image being generated rather than photographed doesn't change what it does to the person depicted — which is why lawmakers and platforms treat it as abuse.
